PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL - ATTORNEY-CLIENT COMMUNICATION / ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT
MEMORANDUM (protective-order-analysis-memo)
TO: James R. Ostrander; David Yamashiro, General Counsel, CIS
RE: United States v. Cascadia Industrial Solutions, Inc., No. 2:25-cv-00482-RAJ (W.D. Wash.) - Analysis of DOJ's May 23, 2025 redline of CIS's proposed Protective Order
KEY DATES: CIS response requested by Fri. June 6, 2025; filing of agreed order or competing proposals (15-page briefs) due June 16; responsive briefs (10 pages) June 23; Halcyon coordination motions due July 31. No discovery may be served or produced until an order is entered (Scheduling Order para. 1), so delay compresses discovery that closes Feb. 27, 2026.

1. BOTTOM LINE
The cover email presents a modest, "standard" markup. It is not. The redline (a) strips the trade-secret tier that protects OptiPrice, (b) lets DOJ use CIS's compelled discovery in any civil, criminal or administrative matter while a grand jury investigation is open, (c) lets DOJ pass AEO material to the FTC and state AGs on five calendar days' notice with the burden on CIS to get a court order, and (d) adds an 18-month automatic de-designation that is unworkable for 3.2 million documents. Several significant changes are not mentioned in the email at all (Section 3). Recommendation: reject items 1-6 below as drafted, offer the compromises in Section 4, give DOJ a written counter by June 6, and prepare competing proposals in parallel. These are the issues that matter to CIS's stated $25-40 million annual leakage exposure and to the risk to individual executives.

2. THRESHOLD CAUTIONS
(a) Baseline mismatch. The redline base is not the May 5 order in our file. Our file version has Sec. 12 (independent-source carve-out; discovery material stays protected), Sec. 13 (no disclosure to FTC, state AGs, co-defendants or cooperators without consent or order, 13.3), a 30-business-day receiving-party challenge window, a 6-month in-house bar, and Exhibit B/C undertakings. The redline base has different numbering, no Sec. 13 equivalent, and a one-sentence parallel clause.  Before responding, confirm which document went out on May 5 and run a full compare; any untracked differences (particularly the omitted co-defendant/cooperator prohibition, original 13.3, and the Section 12.3 rule that discovery material stays protected) must be restored and reserved in writing. Do not accept the redline as the new base without this check.
(b) Authorities. The Jennings rulings come from the internal May 25 survey and were not independently pulled; cite-check before quoting. They are persuasive only. The client memo says "Richard" Jennings; the Scheduling Order says Robert.
(c) Governing law: Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(c)(1)(G); Seattle Times Co. v. Rhinehart, 467 U.S. 20 (1984) (use restrictions need only good cause); W.D. Wash. LCR 26(c)(2) (model order; verify text, site inaccessible) and LCR 5(g). Only Ninth Circuit and Supreme Court law binds.

3. CHANGE-BY-CHANGE ANALYSIS (redline section numbers; severity High/Med/Low)
HIGH
1. Third tier deleted (2.4, 4.1, 5.3, 8.3; Exhibit B to the extent relevant). Effect: OptiPrice source code, algorithms and ~5,700 related documents (4,500 code/development; 1,200 prosecution files) fall to AEO, losing the secure-review room, outside-counsel-only limit, no-copy rule and in-house exclusion, and exposed to the new DOJ access categories. DOJ's rationale ("no patent claims") misses the point: tiers protect trade secrets (Rule 26(c)(1)(G)), not only patent litigation. Per the survey, Judge Jennings approved a third tier in Pacific Aggregate Supply on a categorical showing of DTSA/state-law trade secret status and rejected the argument that government plaintiffs are entitled to a simpler order. CIS needs a declaration (Mr. Yamashiro offered) covering the three patents, the ~$8 million development cost, the air-gapped server, under-15 access list and NDAs. Define the tier narrowly (code, parameters, development records); issued patents disclose methods, so the secret is the implementation. Pricing data and Halcyon communications stay AEO.
2. Use limitation widened (Sec. 1, 7.1) to "this litigation and any related investigation, enforcement action, or regulatory proceeding", plus the new parallel-proceedings clause (Sec. 14) allowing any information "produced in this Action" to be used in any civil, criminal or administrative proceeding. The email says the criminal grand jury investigation remains open. Effect: compelled civil production feeds the criminal case against CIS and its executives.  Law cuts both ways: the government may generally use civil discovery in a criminal case absent bad faith (United States v. Kordel, 397 U.S. 1 (1970); United States v. Stringer, 535 F.3d 929 (9th Cir. 2008)), but courts routinely enter Rule 26(c) use limits (Rhinehart). The 2.7 deletion of "related investigation" is cosmetic because 7.1 and Sec. 14 restore it. 3. Inter-agency sharing (new Sec. 21) and government personnel (5.1(g), 5.2(e)). 21.1 allows disclosure of Confidential and AEO to the FTC and any state AG in a "multistate investigation" on 5 calendar days' notice; 21.2 puts the burden on CIS to obtain an order within that window or be "deemed" to consent; 21.3 binds recipients only "as if" parties, with no names or signed undertakings. 5.1(g)/5.2(e) separately admit unspecified "government agency personnel assisting with the investigation" to AEO without an undertaking, with no connection to the litigation. Five calendar days is unworkable for 3.2 million documents.  Compare original Sec. 13 (no sharing without consent or order) and the survey's reported conditions: named agencies, named individuals, signed undertakings, at least 10 business days' notice, and no AEO sharing without a court order on motion. Also, the prohibition on disclosure to co-defendants and cooperators is not in the redline text we have; Halcyon is reportedly in advanced plea talks and is a competitor and supplier, which makes the gap acute. Redline recital adds that Halcyon is separately negotiating its own terms; the Scheduling Order (para. 10) invites coordination by July 31. Insist that nothing CIS designates reach Halcyon or its counsel except under Court order.
4. Automatic de-designation (new 4.4). All designations expire 18 months after designation unless the producing party serves a document-by-document re-designation with certification; failure means unrestricted use. With ~3.2 million documents this converts protection into a deadline trap and invites sanctions-risk certifications. It also conflicts with the original draft's 17.2 (no automatic expiration). The survey reports Judge Jennings rejected a 24-month version in Northline as "unworkable" and adopted a challenge-driven alternative; 18 months is harsher. Counter with challenge-at-any-time and a response duty.
5. Expert provisions (10.1, 10.3, 10.4, Exhibit B deleted). Notice cut from 10 to 3 days, objection window from 7 to 3 days, standalone undertaking removed, experts "deemed bound" on receipt. Deemed binding of a non-signatory is a weak basis for contempt jurisdiction and loses the Exhibit C personal-jurisdiction consent.  Counter: 10 days' notice with CV and engagement disclosures, 5-business-day objection, signed undertaking, and no access pending objection.
6. Government attorneys exempted (new 9.3, Exhibit A note). DOJ says its attorneys, including EAG, are not "in-house counsel" and are exempt from the undertaking and competitive-decision restrictions; and 5.1/5.2 raise the DOJ in-house count to four (CIS stays at two). Asymmetry is the problem: the stated purpose for four is EAG "economists and attorneys", but economists are not attorneys. Competitive decision-making is the test (Brown Bag Software v. Symantec, 960 F.2d 1465 (9th Cir. 1992)), but undertakings remain essential. Counter: reciprocal numbers (e.g., three each), names and signed Exhibit A, and a bar on use outside this Action.
MEDIUM
7. Prosecution bar deleted (Sec. 11). Original 12-month bar protects OptiPrice patents (which can be attacked through inter partes review) and CIS's pipeline. This is a tradeable item.
8. Clawback (13.2): notice window cut from 15 to 5 business days. Rule 502(d) already protects against waiver, so the window mainly affects use risk; still, with ~2,200 privileged documents intermingled, keep 15 business days from discovery (fallback 10). Do not trade away 502(d) language; note DOJ left it intact.
9. Designation process (6.2, 6.3, 8.3). The email describes a shortened "challenge window" from 30 to 10 business days. The redline actually cuts the producing party's response time to a challenge from 30 to 10 business days, with deemed withdrawal on silence, and cuts meet-and-confer from 7 to 5 days and the deposition designation period from 30 to 10 business days. With AEO default for transcripts, 10 business days is tight but tolerable; the deemed-withdrawal combined with 10 days is a trap given volume. Counter: 14 business days (survey: Judge's stated norm for single-defendant cases) with good-cause extensions, and batching by category for large challenges; deemed withdrawal only after a reminder notice.
10. Return/destroy (15.1, 15.3). 60 to 120 days is acceptable. New 15.3 is not: DOJ is excused from returning or destroying federal records (44 U.S.C. 3301) or anything "subject to litigation hold obligations in other matters" - that phrase is unlimited and reinforces the cross-matter use problem. Accept a records-retention exception limited to material that is a federal record, retained in secure storage, still subject to use restrictions and designations, with notice of the categories retained.
11. Sealing (16.1, 22). DOJ asks for "compelling need" for any sealing. The Ninth Circuit standard actually depends on the motion: compelling reasons for filings attached to dispositive or merits-related motions, but good cause for non-dispositive motions (Kamakana v. City & County of Honolulu, 447 F.3d 1172 (9th Cir. 2006); Center for Auto Safety v. Chrysler Group, LLC, 809 F.3d 1092 (9th Cir. 2016)). The redline imposes the higher standard on everything and adds a "no less restrictive alternative" showing. The email says the provision is "compelled" by Ninth Circuit law; it is not as drafted. Replace with a neutral cross-reference to LCR 5(g) and the governing standard, preserving the producing party's seven business days' notice before a Receiving Party files (original 16.3) and a right to be heard. 22.1 is harmless if it says "applicable standards", but delete 22.2's no-sealing-right language.
LOW: typo fixes and renumbering; the Halcyon recital is acceptable if neutral and paired with a co-defendant bar.

4. CHANGES OMITTED FROM THE COVER EMAIL: government personnel in Tiers 1-2 (5.1(g), 5.2(e)); 9.3 carve-out; 21.2 deemed consent; 15.3 other-matter hold exception; Exhibit B deletion; 3-day objection window; deemed withdrawal after 10 days; loss of independent-source language and the co-defendant/cooperator ban.

5. RECOMMENDED RESPONSE (priority order, aligned with client memo Priorities 1-5)
Must-haves: (1) third tier for narrowly defined OptiPrice/code materials with categorical description at designation; (2) use limited to this Action (fallback: DOJ may seek leave on notice to use specific material in a named proceeding); (3) no sharing outside the DOJ trial team without named recipients, signed undertakings, 10 business days' notice, and a court order for AEO/tier 3; and no disclosure to co-defendants/cooperators absent order; (4) no automatic de-designation.
Tradeable: 120-day return; records-retention exception as narrowed; 14-business-day response; sealing language tracking LCR 5(g); prosecution bar narrowed; clawback at 10 business days; expert notice of 7-10 days.
Process: (i) By May 30, confirm baseline and send a short cover letter correcting the email's descriptions (challenge-window, "compelling need", "adequate safeguard"). (ii) Meet and confer during the week of June 2 (offer firm dates, since DOJ said it would propose them); (iii) respond by June 6 with a counter-redline; (v) begin drafting the 15-page brief and the Yamashiro declaration now, since the June 16 filing is firm and no discovery moves until entry; (vi) consider requesting a Rule 16 or telephonic discovery conference (Scheduling Order para. 11, three-page joint letter) if DOJ refuses to move on use and sharing; (vii) loop in criminal counsel for individuals; (viii) coordinate with Halcyon's counsel only through privileged, appropriate common-interest channels, given its reported cooperation posture, and raise the July 31 coordination deadline.
Risk: CIS is strongest on items 1, 3 and 4; weakest on a flat ban on other-proceeding use and on government-attorney undertakings, where the Court may craft conditions.
LIMITS: Only the supplied documents and limited web checks were used; case citations other than Chrysler/Kamakana (confirmed via search for Chrysler) are from memory and must be cite-checked, as must LCR 26(c)(2)/5(g).
